Limited partnerships (LPs) and limited liability partnerships (LLPs) are both businesses with more than one owner, but unlike general partnerships, limited partnerships and limited liability partnerships offer some of their owners limited personal liability for business debts. In limited partnerships (LPs), at least one of the owners is considered a "general" partner who makes business decisions and is personally liable for business debts. But LPs also have at least one "limited" partner who invests money in the business but has minimal control over daily business decisions and operations. The advantage for these limited partners is that they are not personally liable for business debts. The limited liability partnership (LLP) is a similar business structure but it has no general partners. All of the owners of an LLP have limited personal liability for business debts. In order to better understand LPs and LLPs, it's helpful to compare them to general partnerships. In the business world, the word "partnership" usually refers to general partnerships. A general partnership is a business that has more than one owner and that has not filed papers with the state to create a specific entity such as a corporation or limited liability company (LLC). (Click here to learn more about general partnerships.) In a general partnership: A limited partnership has at least one general partner and at least one limited partner. The general partner has the same role as in a general partnership: controlling the company's day-to-day operations and being personally liable for business debts. The role of limited partners, however, differs in a few ways: Limited partners need to understand that they can become personally liable if they do not stick to their passive role. If a limited partner starts taking an active role in the business, that partner's liability can become unlimited. If a creditor can prove that a limited partner took acts that led the creditor to believe that he or she was a general partner, that partner can be held fully and personally liable for the creditor's claims. Some states have carved out exceptions to this "active role in the business" rule. These exceptions usually allow a limited partner to vote on issues that affect the basic structure of the partnership, including the removal of general partners, terminating the partnership, amending the partnership agreement, or selling all or most of the assets of the partnership, without jeopardizing limited partner status. Another kind of partnership, called a limited liability partnership (LLP) or sometimes called a registered limited liability partnership (RLLP), provides all of its owners with limited personal liability. LLPs are particularly well-suited to professional groups, such as lawyers and accountants. In fact, in some states LLPs are only available to professionals. Professionals often prefer LLPs to general partnerships, corporations, or LLCs because they don't want to be personally liable for another partner's problems -- particularly those involving malpractice claims. An LLP protects each partner from debts against the partnership arising from professional malpractice lawsuits against another partner. (A partner who loses a malpractice suit for his own mistakes, however, doesn't escape liability.) Forming a corporation to protect personal assets may be too much trouble. In addition, some states (including California) won't allow licensed professionals to form an LLC. An LLC is similar to a limited partnership in that it provides liability protection to the owners of the business, and the owners have flexibility in deciding how the business will be managed. However, unlike limited partnerships, all of the owners of the LLC have limited liability protection. For more information, check out LLCs and Limited Liability Protection. In addition, states typically have different formation paperwork for LLCs than for LPs. Further, while partnerships use partnership agreements to delegate rights and responsibilities, LLCs use operating agreements to outline the internal operating procedures. To learn more about choosing between an LLC and an LLP, check out LLC vs. LLP: What Is the Difference? Creating a limited partnership or limited liability partnership is done at the state level. Each state has its own rules, but in general, you must pay a fee and file papers with the state, usually a "certificate of limited partnership" or "certificate of limited liability partnership." This document is similar to the articles (or certificate) filed by a corporation or an LLC and includes information about the general and limited partners. Filing fees for LPs and LLPs are similar to those for corporations and LLCs. Many small business owners can form an LP or LLP on their own. However, if you have legal questions or want to better understand your options and what works best for your business, consider talking to a local business lawyer. All About the Lis Pendens ---by SolonPhillips, Esq. Many people have asked, “So what’s this lis pendens about?” This article will answer the question. And if you’ve never heard the words “lis pendens”before, well, read this article and you will know exactly what it is if and when you do hear it. And if you’re in real estate, then you will hear it or you should hear it. If you have anything to do with real estate then knowing what a lis pendens is and what it is not will benefit you. Period. So here it goes. Lis pendens This is a Latin word that literally means, “a suit pending.” This is the very first thing you need to know about a lis pendens—it means that there is “a suit pending.” A lis pendens is written notice that there is a suit pending. But what does that mean and why should you care? Well, every time you go to buy or sell a house or a building, there is a title or a deed associated with the house or building. The title or deed is a document showing who is the current owner of the house. Whomever you are buying the house from must have a title or deed to the house or else they cannot sell you the house. So how do you know who or what is on the deed or title of the house? You know this by pulling the title report. The title report to a house or building is something very much like a medical record or better yet, a CarFax report. Most people are familiar with the commercial for CarFax. Someone says, “show me the CarFax!” meaning show me the written history of the car so I can see all the accidents, odometer readings,salvage/junk title—show me everything that ever went on with the car and is going on with this car. Show me the CarFax report. The title to a house is similar to a CarFax in that it shows the potential buyer what went on with the ownership of the house and what is going on with the ownership. In comes the lis pendens. The lis pendens is a written notice that goes on the title of a house or real estate property to tell the world, “there is a pending suit” on this house you are about to buy or sell. Why is that important?--because once the lis pendens is placed on the title, the buyer is put on notice that if he or she buys this house, he risks the chance of losing the house after the purchase because the house is “pending a lawsuit.” This means that even though you may have bought the house and think that you own the house, if the person who has filed suit to gain this house wins, you will lose the house—and all the money you put into the house. Ouch! It works something like this. Say you are looking for a house. You’re looking, looking, looking and then boom! You find what seems to be the perfect house. Right there on Zillow, you find it. You call your realtor. Your realtor gives you the rundown and then promptly sets up a time for you to view the house. You and your spouse go to the house and it is everything you have ever wanted. The home has four bedrooms with a master-bedroom on the first floor--this was a must because your knees are bad and you can’t deal with too many stairs. It has a full basement with 9 feet ceilings—this is important because your spouse is a sports fanatic and has huge parties and the basement is the perfect place to host loud, rambunctious get-togethers. The kitchen, oh my! The kitchen is the largest, most spacious kitchen you’ve ever seen, equipped with an island,double oven, and tile floors made of something that looks like grey marble. You absolutely love this house. You love it! And even more than that, the house is in your price range--$500,000. It’s a steal! This house appraises for$550,000, which means it already has $50,000 equity in it. If your offer is accepted you are ahead of the game. So you instruct your realtor to put in an offer. You go back and forth with your realtor, who is going back and forth with the Seller’s realtor: how much closing help will they give? No, that’s not enough. Can we have a 5-day inspection period? Will they give credit for repairs? Can we close sooner? yada, yada, yada—finally, after what seems like weeks of back and forth, your realtor tells you that your offer for $500,000 is accepted. Woooohoooo!!! You are winning! You were pre-approved for $505,000 before you even found the house so you already know that your financing is in place. You are ready to close, and you could not be more excited. As closing day approaches, your realtor contacts you and tells you—a day before closing—that the title report came back and there is a“cloud” on the title. You say, “A what?” Your realtor says again, “a cloud—there is a cloud on the title.” You say, “What does that mean? A cloud? Is it going to rain on my house?” “No, no. A cloud. There is a lis pendens on the title.” Ah! A lis pendens. Right. How Did It Get There? So your beloved house has a lis pendens on it. How did the lis pendens come to cloud the title to your house? This is how. The guy who is selling you your house used to live in the house with his soon to bee-wife. The couple had a few too many rough spots and the wife decided to leave the husband. She moved out of the house and out of the state. While she was out of the state, the husband filed for divorce and decided to sell the house. He reasoned that it was his house to sell. The problem is, the house was not his to sell. Typically, property purchased and owned during the marriage is marital property and requires both the husband and wife to agree to sell the house or have a court force the sale of the house. But the wife was away. She was not communicating with her husband. The husband did not want the house, but he could sure use the money, especially since there was no mortgage on the home. So he figured, with wife away, with her not communicating with him, why not? He’ll just sell the house and move on with his life and his$500,000. Perfect plan. Not so perfect plan. When the wife realized the husband was planning on selling the house, her house, guess what she does? She filed a lis pendens—a simple one-page document that is filed in the land records department located in the county courthouse where the house is located. Her simple filing places world is on notice that her house is subject to a pending lawsuit and if you buy it, you buy at your own risk. And with the lis pendens goes your hopes and dreams. Why? Because if you get a loan to buy this house (if your bank even lends you the money—most banks will not bother lending you the money with a lis pendens on the title) and you buy the house, move into the house, if the person who put the lis pendens wins the lawsuit, then the winner of the lawsuit can reclaim his/her house and have you evicted. Why? Because you purchased the house subject to a lis pendens. You purchased a house knowing good and well you might lose it. You took a $500,000 risk and lost. This is the power of a lis pendens. An LP (limited partnership) is a popular type of investment vehicle used mainly by institutional and wealthy investors. Unlike a limited liability company (SARL), where each partner is responsible for the company's debts and liabilities, the LP is a limited partnership, i.e. the general partners have unlimited liability and the special partners have limited liability. An LP consists of a general partner (usually a private equity fund) responsible for investing and operating assets, and one or more special partners responsible for providing capital. The funds raised from the contribution of the special partners are pooled into a single legal entity. Special partners are typically financial institutions and pension funds that invest capital with LPs and are remunerated by an annual distribution rate and capital gains participation. In general, the returns special partners receive are predetermined by the LP contract, which defines the amount and timing of distributions they are to receive. LPs have become a very popular way for institutional investors and wealthy investors to invest in the private sector. LPs enable companies and private equity funds to raise capital more efficiently, as special investors agree to repay them out of their profits. A Limited Partnership (LP) is a unique business structure that blends the strategic management of general partners with the investment potential of limited partners. Unlike other business structures, LPs offer distinct advantages, including limited liability for investors and pass-through taxation. This is a recommended structure for business owners who want to raise capital and maintain operational control and for investors who look for lower-risk opportunities. Business people and investors can make informed decisions that align with their goals if they understand the LP structure, its primary purposes, and how it contrasts with other entities such as LLCs, LLPs, and GPs. Understanding Limited Partnerships (LPs) A Limited Partnership is a business structure with at least one general partner and at least one limited partner. General partners run the business and assume unlimited financial liability, while limited partners contribute capital and enjoy limited liability. This dual-tiered approach offers a strategic balance between active management and passive investment. General partners in an LP are responsible for the day-to-day business operations, while limited partners primarily invest in the business and receive a profit share without being involved in management. Key Features of a Limited Partnership - Mix of General and Limited Partners: An LP requires at least one general partner and one or more limited partners. - Limited Liability for Investors: Limited partners’ liability is restricted to the extent of their investment, which attracts passive investors. - Pass-Through Taxation Advantages: Profits and losses are reported on personal tax returns, which often reduces the overall tax burden for the partners. - Popular Use Cases: LPs are commonly used in investment funds, real estate ventures, and specific business arrangements where capital investment is needed without active management participation. Limited Partnership vs. Other Business Structures Why should you opt for an LP rather than a General Partnership, a Limited Liability Partnership, or a Limited Liability Company? Let’s see the main differences between the structures. LP vs. General Partnership (GP) - Liability: In a GP, each partner is personally responsible for the business’s obligations (unlimited liability). In contrast, LPs offer limited liability to passive investors and protect limited partners from financial risks beyond their initial investment. - Management Roles: In GPs, all partners are typically involved in management and decision-making. LPs designate management exclusively to general partners, and limited partners make investments without direct involvement in operations. - Risk and Involvement: GPs require all partners to take an active role, while LPs provide a safer investment route for those who prefer minimal management duties. LP vs. Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) - Legal Protection: In an LLP, all partners benefit from liability protection, and their personal assets are shielded from business debts and legal claims. LPs, by contrast, only offer limited liability to limited partners, leaving general partners exposed to unlimited liability. - Management Flexibility: LPs restrict limited partners from participating in management, while LLPs allow all partners to participate in management decisions without sacrificing liability protection. - Use Cases: LPs are typically utilized for investment purposes and passive income opportunities, whereas LLPs are more common among professional service firms, such as law practices and accounting firms, where all partners may contribute to management. LP vs. Limited Liability Company (LLC) - Ownership and Taxation: LLCs provide limited liability to all members and offer significant flexibility in management structures. LLC members can participate in management without losing liability protection, unlike in LPs where only general partners manage the business. Both structures benefit from pass-through taxation, but LLCs can also select corporate tax treatment if advantageous. - Situational Preference: LPs are preferred when there is a clear division between management and investment, such as in real estate investment funds or private equity ventures. LLCs are better suited for small businesses or startups where owners want both operational involvement and liability protection. How to Form a Limited Partnership (LP) Setting up an LP is easy – especially if you rely on professional assistance. Here are the steps you will have to take. Choosing the Right Jurisdiction - Regulatory Variances: LP formation regulations differ by country and state, influencing the ease of setup, ongoing compliance, and potential tax benefits. You will need to research and choose a jurisdiction with favorable business laws that align with the partnership’s objectives. - Popular Jurisdictions: The U.S., Canada, and offshore regions like the Cayman Islands and Luxembourg are popular choices due to favorable tax laws, robust legal protections, and established frameworks for managing limited partnerships effectively. You may be interested in taking a detailed look at the most popular jurisdictions: Drafting a Partnership Agreement Key components include: - Responsibilities of general and limited partners - Profit and loss distribution - Decision-making processes within the partnership - Conflict resolution procedures - Guidelines for adding or removing partners - Terms for dissolving the partnership if necessary. - Filing Requirements: Businesses must register with local or national authorities by submitting a Certificate of Limited Partnership. You will need to provide essential information, such as the partnership’s name, principal place of business, and details of all partners involved. - Costs and Documentation: The registration process includes administrative fees and may require additional documents such as the partnership agreement and identification of partners. Some regions also mandate annual renewals and compliance reporting. Obtaining Necessary Licenses & Permits - Industry-Specific Compliance: Financial services, healthcare, and construction businesses are just a few examples of industries that need special regulatory approvals to operate legally. Compliance with industry standards and regulations can prevent legal issues and promote smooth operations. Advantages and Disadvantages of a Limited Partnership It is important to consider the benefits and drawbacks of a Limited Partnership with due care before you make a decision to set it up. Advantages of a Limited Partnership - Limited Liability for Passive Investors: Limited partners are not responsible for business debts and obligations beyond their investment. - Pass-Through Taxation Benefits: Avoids double taxation as profits are reported on personal tax returns. - Investment Opportunities: Suitable for real estate projects and investment funds. Disadvantages of a Limited Partnership - Unlimited Liability for General Partners: General partners bear full responsibility for business debts and obligations. - Management Restrictions: Limited partners cannot engage in day-to-day business operations. - Compliance Costs: Legal and regulatory compliance may involve high costs. Limited Partnership and Taxation Partnerships are often set up to take advantage of convenient taxation rules. Let’s take a detailed look at them. How LPs Are Taxed - Pass-Through Taxation: LPs do not pay corporate taxes as profits and losses are passed through to personal tax returns. - Tax Obligations: General partners must pay self-employment taxes, while limited partners may have different obligations. Tax Benefits of LPs - Avoiding Double Taxation: Income is taxed at the individual level only. - Expense Deductions: Potential to deduct business expenses on personal tax returns. LP Taxation in Different Countries - Regional Differences: The U.S. offers specific tax advantages, while offshore jurisdictions may provide favorable conditions for international investors. When Should You Choose a Limited Partnership? Is Limited Partnership an ideal business structure that suits everyone under any conditions? No, it is not. However, there are cases when it is indispensable. Ideal Business Models for LPs - Investment Funds: LPs are ideal for private equity and venture capital funds where passive investors contribute capital while general partners manage investment strategies. - Real Estate Ventures: Real estate developers can use the LP model to raise funds from limited partners, which reduces their personal financial risks while driving large-scale projects forward. - Family Businesses: The structure helps in succession planning as it enables limited partners (often family members) to hold ownership interests without participating in daily management. Who Benefits the Most from an LP? - Investors: Those who seek limited liability and passive income opportunities benefit significantly from LPs. Limited partners can invest in high-potential business ventures, real estate projects, or private equity funds while protecting their personal assets from business debts. - Entrepreneurs: Business owners who need investment without giving up management control find LPs advantageous. Entrepreneurs can access necessary capital from limited partners and retain the authority to make critical business decisions. - Professional Managers: LPs also excellent for professional managers who act as general partners in investment funds. They actively manage the fund’s portfolio and attract investment from individuals/institutions that seek a passive role. Common Risks and How to Mitigate Them A business structure that does not carry any risks simply does not exist. A far-sighted entrepreneur is familiar with possible risks and knows how to mitigate them. Liability Risks for General Partners - Financial Exposure: General partners are personally liable for corporate debts and obligations. That is, if the LP incurs debt or faces legal action, the personal assets owned by general partners could be at risk. - Mitigation Strategies: General partners can mitigate these risks by purchasing liability insurance to cover potential losses and legal fees. In addition, some may consider restructuring as an LLP or an LLC to reduce personal liability and maintain control over the business at the same time. Disputes Between Partners - Conflict Resolution: Disputes can arise over profit distribution, management decisions, or exit strategies. A well-drafted partnership agreement is crucial in managing disputes effectively. - Preventive Measures: Communicate on a regular basis, keep transparent financial records, and set clear expectations for general and limited partners to avoid misunderstandings and conflicts. Compliance and Regulatory Challenges - Avoiding Legal Issues: LPs must keep track of any changes in tax, reporting, and compliance requirements. Failures to do so may entail fines, legal penalties, and potential loss of limited liability status for limited partners. All these risks can be managed by engaging professional legal and accounting advisors. - Documentation and Record-Keeping: Keep detailed records of communications with officials, financial operations, and partnership agreements to easily prove that your business is transparent. Conclusion A Limited Partnership is definitely a unique business structure where investment opportunities are combined with operational control. It is an option-not-to-miss for business owners who want to attract passive investors and make strategic decisions at the same time. LPs are a highly recommended structure if you engage in real estate, investment funds, and family businesses where a clear separation between management and investment is beneficial. However, prospective partners must carefully consider the risks, especially the unlimited liability borne by general partners. If you want to successfully establish an LP, you will need to choose the right jurisdiction, draft a detailed partnership agreement, and maintain compliance with regulatory requirements. In addition, make sure you understand the tax implications and the concept of pass-through taxation. A well-structured LP will create a stable framework for business operations that will help your business grow and benefit from better investment opportunities.
